cards.back: A measure space is a triple $(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mu)$, where $\Omega$ is a set, $\mathcal{F}$ is a $\sigma$-algebra on $\Omega$, and $\mu:\mathcal{F}\to[0,\infty]$ is a measure.
A probability space is a measure space with total mass $1$: $(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P})$, where $\mathbb{P}:\mathcal{F}\to[0,1]$ is a probability measure and $\mathbb{P}(\Omega)=1$.
The sample space $\Omega$ is the set of all possible outcomes. An individual outcome is written $\omega\in\Omega$.

A $\sigma$-algebra $\mathcal{F}\subseteq\mathcal{P}(\Omega)$ satisfies: $\Omega\in\mathcal{F}$; if $A\in\mathcal{F}$, then $A^c\in\mathcal{F}$; and if $A_1,A_2,\dots\in\mathcal{F}$, then $\bigcup_{n=1}^{\infty}A_n\in\mathcal{F}$.

A measure is a function $\mu:\mathcal{F}\to[0,\infty]$ such that $\mu(\varnothing)=0$ and, for pairwise disjoint $A_1,A_2,\dots\in\mathcal{F}$, $\mu\left(\bigcup_{n=1}^{\infty}A_n\right)=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\mu(A_n)$.
A probability measure is a measure $\mathbb{P}:\mathcal{F}\to[0,1]$ such that $\mathbb{P}(\Omega)=1$.

cards.front: Define a real-valued random variable formally.
cards.back: A real-valued random variable is a measurable map $X:(\Omega,\mathcal{F})\to(\mathbb{R},\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}))$, i.e. $X^{-1}(B)\in\mathcal{F}$ for every Borel set $B\in\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})$. Equivalently (checking on a generating set): $\{X\le x\} \in \mathcal{F}$ for every $x\in\mathbb{R}$.

cards.front: Define a random variable less formally.
cards.back: A rule that turns each outcome $\omega$ into a number $X(\omega)$, built so that for any set Borel set $B$ you care about, the outcomes mapping into $B$ form an event, so you can ask `what is the probability of ending up in $B$?`

cards.front: Define the distribution (law) of a real-valued random variable $X$.
cards.back: The law of $X$ is the probability measure $P_X$ on $\mathbb{R}$ given by $$P_X(B)=\mathbb{P}(X\in B)=\mathbb{P}(X^{-1}(B))$$ for Borel sets $B\subseteq\mathbb{R}$. This is answering `whats the probability the random variable $X$ lands in $B$?`

cards.front: Define the expectation of a real-valued random variable $X$.
What is the expectation of a discrete real-valued random variable $X$?
cards.back: $$\mathbb{E}[X]= \sum_{x\in X(\Omega)} x\,\mathbb{P}(X=x) = \sum_{x\in\mathbb{R}} x\,\mathbb{P}(X=x),$$ provided the sum is well-defined.

cards.front: Define a probability density function (PDF) of a real-valued random variable $X$.
cards.back: A probability density function (PDF), or density, is a function $f:\mathbb{R}\to[0,\infty)$ such that $$\mathbb{P}(X\in B)=\int_B f(x)\,dx$$ for every Borel set $B\subseteq\mathbb{R}$. It is unique almost everywhere, but may or may not exist.

cards.front: If a real-valued random variable $X$ has density $f$, what is its expectation?
cards.back: $$\mathbb{E}[X]=\int_{\mathbb{R}} x\,f(x)\,dx,$$ provided the integral is well-defined.

cards.front: Define the cumulative distribution function (CDF) of a real-valued random variable $X$.
cards.back: The CDF of $X$ is the function $F_X:\mathbb{R}\to[0,1]$ defined by $$F_X(t)=\mathbb{P}(X\le t)=P_X((-\infty,t]).$$ It records the probability mass accumulated up to $t$.

cards.front: How does the CDF give probabilities of half-open intervals?
cards.back: For $a<b$, $$\mathbb{P}(a<X\le b)=F_X(b)-F_X(a).$$ This follows because $\{X\le b\}$ is the disjoint union of $\{X\le a\}$ and $\{a<X\le b\}$.
